_comment: The report's cumulative section, one entry per aggregate. Each entry names the tree it describes, so a figure that has fallen behind the branch says so in the rendered table instead of relying on someone remembering. `file` is a perf/scripts/compare_screen.py output under perf/baselines/; `figures` is for an aggregate that is not screen output.
_stock_comment: The commit the stock arm of every aggregate here was measured against. verify_report.py asserts the ref still resolves to it: if next moves, the figures describe a tree that no longer exists and want re-measuring, which should fail a check rather than be noticed by someone eventually.

aggregates.coverage: 57 scenarios on both arms, all 200 bar the deliberate 404 control; Tier 2 timed 57 of 57 on every leg
aggregates.label: Read loop, 57 scenarios
aggregates.note:
median of five alternating rounds per arm with the arm ORDER reversed on even rounds, both arms proved distinct by content hash -- stock `7b5b5d196b78`, branch `c49463c7c02e` -- and each hash reproduced on every arm of every round. Query counts were bit-identical across both deterministic rounds on both arms (3,619 and 897): zero unstable counts in any run, and Tier 2 timed 57 of 57 endpoints on all ten legs.

**Wall clock is the median of each scenario across the five rounds, then summed** -- not the median of the five round totals. Summing rounds first lets the single largest endpoint drive the result, and `api.interface.depth1` is large enough to do it.

Dispersion across rounds is **0.15% on stock and 0.09% on branch**, as the interquartile range of the round totals against their median; max-min is 0.33% and 0.61%. **Per scenario the median scenario's relative standard deviation across rounds is 0.76% on stock and 1.08% on branch.** That is tighter than this row has previously carried, on the same instrument and host; what changed in the conditions is not established, so it is reported rather than explained. The totals remain the figure to quote either way: they are stable because 57 scenarios' errors cancel, so this cumulative number carries weight that an individual per-endpoint wall-clock figure taken from it does not.

**Measured 2026-09-28 against `next` at 0735993cc**, after both perf branches were rebased onto it. The stock arm reproduced 3,619 queries exactly, unchanged across 19 upstream commits. The branch arm reads **897 where it previously read 901**; the difference is on the branch side only and is not yet attributed to a commit.

**The deterministic instruments and the over-HTTP leg were taken in separate sessions the same day**, with the arms re-swapped between them. The first Tier 2 attempt ran without a session cookie, so every UI view answered 302 to /login/, the probe refused to time a redirect, and all ten legs timed 1 endpoint of 57; that attempt was discarded in full and re-run. The tier1 counts and the in-process bench were unaffected -- they drive the Django test client and never present a cookie.

The scenario set is hand-picked and largely what this branch optimised, so it describes these pages fairly rather than predicting an arbitrary one; the read screen row is the unbiased check

aggregates.label: Read screen, every REST read endpoint
aggregates.note:
median of three alternating rounds per arm with the arm ORDER reversed between rounds, enumerated from the URL resolver at run time rather than from a scenario list, and matched on `(id, kind)` -- the kinds make 518 measurements, and keying on id alone collapses them to 165 and silently changes every total. Arms proved distinct by content hash on every swap.

**Direction, not just the net: 51 measurements improved, 334 unchanged, 133 worse.** The 133 are finding 62's trade made visible -- a prefetch replacing a JOIN is more round trips, each cheaper -- and that finding's own note says the query counter reads it as a regression and must not be the gate. They cost 248 queries against 10,368 saved, 2.4%, and the same rounds put database time down 41.2%.

This row exists to check whether the read loop's result generalises beyond the 57 scenarios this branch optimised. It is REST-only -- no UI page appears in it -- and it is a screening instrument read as a ranked list, not a gate

aggregates.label: Write screen, every POST endpoint
aggregates.note:
median of three alternating rounds per arm, matched on `(id, kind)` rather than id alone -- the three kinds make 257 measurements from 105 endpoints, and keying on id alone collapses them. Arms proved distinct by content hash on every swap.

178 measurements improved, 66 unchanged, 10 worse. **Queries and wall clock come apart on the write path and both belong here**: -17.0% queries against -31.3% wall. Gating on queries alone undervalues the write-path work by roughly 1.8x, because those wins are Python -- serializer reuse, natural-key memoization, a tag cache -- rather than SQL.

All 10 that got worse are `update.x1`, and they cost +20 queries against 3,485 saved. Nine of them are nonetheless faster on wall clock; `extras-api:exporttemplate-list` is the one worse on both, at +1 query and +11.4% wall, which is roughly two standard deviations on a three-round median and has not been probed

aggregates.coverage: 11,572 objects created per arm, across 68 models
aggregates.label: Whole-workflow apply, 11,572 objects
aggregates.note:
**the whole-workflow figure: one `databot apply` per arm, creating 11,572 objects across 68 models, two alternating rounds per arm in the order stock/branch/branch/stock, median.** The database is dropped and recreated from an empty template before every arm, so each run builds the dataset from nothing.

The client runs on a second host, not on the box under measurement: it builds every payload itself and is a sustained CPU load, and the perf overlay commits all eight of the measurement host's threads. Measured cost of moving it off-box is +0.16ms per TCP connect against ~198ms average per request.

Wall clock is tight across rounds -- stock 1838/1835s, branch 1039/1038s, spans of 0.16% and 0.10% -- and row counts were identical on all four arms (536 devices, 1,616 interfaces, 1,648 cables), which is what says each arm applied the same work. Query counts come from `pg_stat_statements` reset per arm, so they cover the whole run rather than one request.

The dataset file defines 11,578 objects and databot reports creating 11,572; the six-object difference was not chased, and the figures here describe what was created. The figures are computed from the run's own result lines by `perf/scripts/compare_apply.py`, so verify_report.py recomputes this row like any other.

This row carries two rounds per arm where it previously carried three. Four arms is what the overnight-refresh sequence in perf/scripts/README.md specifies, and the round-to-round spread above is narrower than the three-round run's was
